name: Vitamin A (retinyl palmitate) from liver

angle.text: Diet communities eat liver or take liver-derived products as a source of preformed vitamin A, aiming for better skin. Vitamin A's role in skin is well known through retinoids; appearance trials of dietary liver have not been run.

summary: Preformed vitamin A from liver is a real nutrient with a documented toxicity threshold; no appearance trials exist.
note: Excess preformed vitamin A is linked to liver damage, bone effects and, per standard guidance, caution in pregnancy.
currentQuick:
Animal liver and some supplements supply preformed vitamin A (retinol and retinyl esters). Some people eat liver for skin and general health.
The sources reviewed contain no trials testing liver-derived vitamin A for appearance. What they do document is toxicity from excess intake.
How it works: Retinyl esters are the animal storage form of vitamin A, held mostly in the liver; once absorbed they supply retinol, which the body uses in vision, skin and growth processes.
Risks and caveats: Hypervitaminosis A can cause nausea, headache, vision changes, skin peeling, hair loss, bone pain and liver damage. US Institute of Medicine upper intake is 3,000 micrograms per day for adults and lower for children; pregnancy and liver disease call for close monitoring of intake.
deepLead:
Preformed vitamin A, which includes retinol and retinyl esters such as retinyl palmitate, occurs in animal liver and in some supplements. Some diet communities eat liver or take liver-derived products for skin, vision and general nutrition. Hypervitaminosis A is the toxicity caused by excess preformed vitamin A, and Wikipedia lists liver, supplements and prescription medicines as the usual sources.
Reported effects of excess intake include nausea, headache, vision changes, skin peeling and dryness, hair loss, bone pain and liver damage, and the condition is most strongly recognised with acute ingestion of very vitamin A-rich livers such as polar bear liver. The US Institute of Medicine tolerable upper intake for adults is 3,000 micrograms per day.

name: Cod liver oil

angle.text: Users take cod liver oil for its vitamin A, vitamin D and omega-3 content, hoping for better skin and general health. Its nutrients are well characterised; appearance outcomes have not been trialled.

summary: A traditional vitamin A, D and omega-3 oil with a long medical history; no appearance trials, and its vitamin A content is the main safety issue.
note: One tablespoon exceeds the adult upper limit for vitamin A and far exceeds limits for young children.
currentQuick:
Cod liver oil is a fish-liver supplement supplying omega-3 fats plus vitamins A and D. It has a long history as a folk and bottled remedy and helped lead to the discovery of vitamins A and D.
No trial was found testing it for appearance outcomes. Human studies have looked at blood lipids, platelet function and childhood outcomes instead.
How it works: EPA and DHA are incorporated into blood and cell lipids with supplementation, as one human study reported. Vitamin D supports bone mineralisation, and its use against rickets is the best-documented historical effect.
Risks and caveats: Vitamin A accumulates in the liver, and Wikipedia reports a tablespoon exceeds the adult tolerable upper limit and children's limits several-fold. Excess preformed vitamin A can cause nausea, skin peeling, bone pain and liver damage.
deepLead:
Cod liver oil is a dietary supplement made from the liver of Atlantic cod (Gadus morhua). Like other fish oils it contains the omega-3 fatty acids EPA and DHA, and unlike most it also contains substantial vitamins A and D. One tablespoon (13.6 g) provides about 4,080 micrograms of vitamin A and 34 micrograms (1,360 IU) of vitamin D according to USDA figures cited by Wikipedia.
It was used in northern European folk medicine for rheumatism and became a bottled remedy in the nineteenth century, and it played a part in the discovery of vitamins A and D. In looksmaxxing and diet communities it is discussed as a vitamin A and D source, often alongside Weston A. Price-style diets.
Trials from the 1980s examined its effects on blood lipids and platelet function, and observational work examined childhood outcomes. The sources reviewed contain no trial testing it for appearance. One tablespoon exceeds the adult tolerable upper intake for vitamin A, which is why vitamin A toxicity is the principal safety concern.

name: Fermented cod liver oil / butter oil (Weston A. Price)

chain: Claimed support for bone and teeth
angle.text: Followers of the Weston A. Price Foundation take this pairing as a source of fat-soluble vitamins, aiming for dental, skeletal and facial-structure benefits. The facial-structure link is a theory with no clinical studies.

summary: A Weston A. Price Foundation supplement pairing of fermented cod liver oil and butter oil; no clinical studies found.
note: Cod liver oil is high in preformed vitamin A; the sources reviewed cover vitamin A toxicity thresholds.
currentQuick:
This is a supplement pairing promoted by followers of dentist Weston A. Price, combining fermented cod liver oil with high-vitamin butter oil as a source of fat-soluble vitamins.
Price's 1939 work on traditional diets drew both praise and criticism from reviewers, and no clinical trials of the combination were found.
How it works: Followers describe the oils as supplying vitamins A and D and related fat-soluble nutrients thought to support teeth and bone structure. Studies testing that for appearance were not found.
Risks and caveats: No studies of this specific pairing were found. Cod liver oil is a concentrated source of preformed vitamin A, for which the US upper intake for adults is 3,000 micrograms per day.
deepLead:
Fermented cod liver oil combined with high-vitamin butter oil is a supplement pairing associated with the Weston A. Price Foundation, a nutrition advocacy group co-founded in 1999 by Sally Fallon and Mary G. Enig to promote the research of Canadian dentist Weston A. Price (1870 to 1948). Followers use it as a source of fat-soluble vitamins, aiming for dental, skeletal and facial-structure benefits.
Price's 1939 book Nutrition and Physical Degeneration described his travels studying traditional diets and argued that processed foods caused deficiencies and disease. Reviewers at the time and since have disagreed about his work: a 1940 Journal of the American Medical Association review called his approach evangelistic rather than scientific, while a Canadian Medical Association Journal review praised it. The sources reviewed contain no clinical studies of the fermented cod liver oil and butter oil combination.

name: Weston A. Price diet

chain: Traditional foods, no refined flour or sugar
Claimed better dental and jaw development
angle.text: Proponents follow this traditional-foods diet based on a 1930s dentist's comparisons of teeth and facial development, believing it supports facial structure and fewer cavities. The diet itself has not been trialled for appearance.

summary: Traditional-foods philosophy from a 1930s dentist's travels; influential in diet circles, with no trials of the diet itself.
note: Based on Price's observational surveys, which later reviewers criticised for lacking controls.
currentQuick:
The Weston A. Price diet is a set of traditional-foods ideas drawn from dentist Weston A. Price's 1939 book comparing the teeth and faces of traditional and Westernised peoples. Followers connect refined sugar, flour and processed fats with dental decay and facial development.
Price's book drew early praise and later criticism for lacking quantitative analysis and controls. No clinical trials of the diet as a whole were found.
How it works: The central claim is that nutrient-dense traditional foods support normal tooth and jaw development, while processed foods cause deficiency. This is based on Price's observational comparisons, not on controlled experiments.
Risks and caveats: No specific harms were identified in the sources reviewed. Critics focus on the weak evidence base of Price's surveys and, separately, on his earlier focal infection theory, which was discredited by later reviews.
deepLead:
The Weston A. Price diet is a "traditional foods" dietary philosophy derived from the work of Weston A. Price (1870-1948), a Canadian-born American dentist who compared the diets, teeth and facial development of traditional and Westernised populations in his 1939 book Nutrition and Physical Degeneration. Proponents draw on it to argue that refined flour, sugar and industrial vegetable fats lead to dental decay and narrower facial structure, themes that overlap with appearance-focused communities.
Price's nutrition work was received with both praise and criticism. Contemporary reviewers described the book as a masterpiece or as evangelistic rather than scientific, and later critics said it lacked quantitative dietary analysis and control groups. The wiki found no clinical trials of a Weston A. Price diet as a whole.

name: Ray Peat diet

angle.text: Followers eat milk, fruit, juice and saturated fats to raise metabolism and correct hormone balance, aiming for a leaner, healthier look. Support comes from Peat's writings and anecdote; there are no trials.

summary: Dairy, fruit, juice and low-PUFA eating from Raymond Peat's writings; popular for hormone claims, with no trials.
note: Hormone and height claims come from forum anecdotes; none have been tested in published studies.
currentQuick:
The Ray Peat diet is built around milk, fruit and juice, root vegetables, eggs, shellfish and saturated fats while avoiding polyunsaturated fats. Followers say it raises metabolism and balances hormones.
No clinical trials of the diet were found. Forum discussion mixes enthusiastic reports with scepticism.
How it works: Proponents say lowering PUFA intake and eating sugar-rich, dairy-rich foods supports thyroid function and metabolic rate and lowers estrogen. These mechanisms have not been tested in published studies of the diet.
Risks and caveats: No harms were documented in the sources reviewed. Users in forums mention hormone-related side effects anecdotally, and extreme claims such as height gain are unsupported by published research.
deepLead:
The Ray Peat diet is an eating pattern inspired by the writings of Raymond Peat, an American author on nutrition and physiology. Followers describe it as "pro-metabolic" and aimed at correcting hormonal imbalances and raising metabolic rate. Typical elements are milk, cheese, fruit and fruit juice, root vegetables, eggs, shellfish, muscle and organ meats, collagen, and saturated fats such as butter and coconut oil, while polyunsaturated fats are avoided.
On looksmax.org the diet is discussed alongside claims about hormones, thyroid function and even height. No clinical trials of the diet were found in the sources reviewed, and the wiki records community claims as claims.

name: Low-PUFA diet

chain: Cut seed oils, nuts, fatty fish
angle.text: Ray Peat followers avoid polyunsaturated fats on the theory that they oxidise and burden metabolism, hoping for better skin and body composition. The idea is untested as an appearance strategy.

summary: Cutting seed oils, nuts and fatty fish on oxidation grounds; popular in Ray Peat circles, untested as a looks strategy.
note: Omega-3 and omega-6 are essential fatty acids; the appearance claims have not been studied.
currentQuick:
A low-PUFA diet avoids polyunsaturated fats from seed oils, nuts, seeds and fatty fish, favouring butter and coconut oil. It is most associated with followers of Ray Peat.
PUFAs do oxidise more easily than other fats in oils, but no trials have tested avoiding them for appearance or metabolic aims.
How it works: Followers say PUFAs oxidise and burden metabolism. Chemistry supports that PUFAs are more oxidation-prone; the health consequences of normal intake are debated.
Risks and caveats: Linoleic and alpha-linolenic acids are essential nutrients and DHA supports brain and retinal function, so reference sources note the need for some intake. No specific harms of low-PUFA eating were identified in the sources.
deepLead:
A low-PUFA diet is an eating pattern that minimises polyunsaturated fatty acids, found in vegetable seed oils, nuts, seeds and fatty fish. In online metabolism and appearance circles it is most associated with the Ray Peat diet, whose followers say PUFAs are unstable, oxidise easily and burden metabolism.
Chemically, PUFAs are more prone to lipid peroxidation and rancidity than saturated or monounsaturated fats. Public health guidance generally treats unsaturated fats as the preferred fats, and omega-3 and omega-6 acids are essential nutrients. The sources reviewed contain no clinical trials of deliberately minimising PUFA for appearance or metabolic goals.

name: Anti-estrogen diet (cruciferous / DIM)

angle.text: Users in T-optimization circles eat broccoli and similar vegetables or take DIM to lower estrogen activity and raise the testosterone-to-estrogen ratio for a leaner, more masculine look. No trial in men shows a visible change.

summary: Eating broccoli or taking DIM to cut estrogen: popular in T-optimization circles, but no trial in men shows it changes anything visible.
note: Evidence on cruciferous vegetables is mostly cancer research, not hormone studies in men.
currentQuick:
The anti-estrogen diet means eating more cruciferous vegetables or taking DIM, a compound derived from them, in the belief that it lowers estrogen and favours testosterone.
Cruciferous vegetables are studied for cancer and detoxification enzymes. The sources reviewed describe no clinical trial testing the hormone claim.
How it works: DIM forms when indole-3-carbinol from these vegetables is digested. Lab studies show it acts on several cell pathways, but how this translates to estrogen levels in men has not been shown in published trials found here.
Risks and caveats: Pure DIM carries irritation hazard labels; supplement safety trials are not described in the sources. It is sold as a dietary supplement.
deepLead:
The anti-estrogen diet is a lifestyle practice in which people eat cruciferous vegetables such as broccoli, cabbage, kale and Brussels sprouts, or take supplements of diindolylmethane (DIM), with the stated aim of lowering estrogen activity or shifting estrogen metabolism, usually in order to raise the ratio of testosterone to estrogen. DIM is a compound formed in the body from indole-3-carbinol, which comes from these vegetables, and it is sold as a dietary supplement.
Research on cruciferous vegetables has centred on glucosinolates and their breakdown products, studied mainly for cancer prevention. An umbrella review reported suggestive evidence of benefit for some cancers and all-cause mortality, and the vegetables are known to induce the liver enzyme CYP1A2. The Wikipedia articles on DIM and cruciferous vegetables do not describe any trial showing that these foods or DIM change estrogen levels or appearance in men.

name: Testosterone-boosting diet (eggs, oysters, red meat)

chain: Support for muscle and masculine features
angle.text: Looksmaxxing and fitness circles eat these foods to support testosterone, muscularity and masculine features. Correcting nutrient deficiencies is known to matter; the diet has not been shown to raise testosterone in men who are already replete.

summary: Eggs, oysters and beef as a T booster: nutrient deficiencies matter, but no trial shows the diet lifts testosterone in men who are already replete.
note: Zinc supplements above sufficiency do not raise testosterone, per Wikipedia.
currentQuick:
This is the belief that eating eggs, oysters and red meat raises testosterone. Zinc, vitamin D and dietary fat are the nutrients usually invoked.
Deficiency in some nutrients lowers testosterone, but the sources describe no trial of this specific diet.
How it works: Zinc is needed for testosterone production, and low-fat diets may lower levels. Food supplies these nutrients; effects beyond correcting a shortfall are not shown.
Risks and caveats: Raw shellfish carries bacterial food-safety risks. No specific harms of the diet itself are described in the sources.
deepLead:
The testosterone-boosting diet is a food-based approach in which people emphasise eggs, oysters, red meat and similar foods, marketed or believed to raise testosterone. It is discussed in looksmaxxing and fitness circles as a way to support muscularity, masculine features and energy.
Wikipedia's testosterone article reports that deficiencies of vitamin A and zinc may lower testosterone, that vitamin D intakes of roughly 400 to 1000 IU per day were associated with higher levels, and that evidence on dietary fat is limited, with low-fat diets possibly lowering total and free testosterone. It also states that zinc supplementation beyond sufficiency has no effect on serum testosterone. No source reviewed shows that a foods-only diet raises testosterone in men who are not deficient.

name: Oysters / shellfish for zinc

angle.text: Oysters are eaten as the richest food source of zinc, a mineral linked to testosterone production, to support muscle and masculine development. Benefit is tied to correcting a deficiency rather than boosting normal levels.

summary: Oysters are the richest food source of zinc, used as a T-support food; benefit is tied to correcting deficiency.
note: Raw shellfish carries Vibrio and other food-safety risks.
currentQuick:
Oysters pack more zinc than any common food, so they are favoured by people trying to support testosterone.
Zinc deficiency can lower testosterone, but the sources say supplementing beyond sufficiency has no effect on serum testosterone.
How it works: Zinc is needed for testosterone synthesis and many enzymes; oysters simply supply it in food form.
Risks and caveats: Raw oysters can carry dangerous bacteria, especially for immunocompromised people.
deepLead:
Oysters and other shellfish are eaten in looksmaxxing and fitness circles as a concentrated food source of zinc, a mineral linked to testosterone production. Wikipedia describes oysters as having the most zinc of any food, with two oysters (28 g) supplying the US reference daily intake.
Wikipedia states zinc is required to make testosterone and that deficiency can lower it, though it is a poor-marker mineral for blood testing and the US RDA for men is 11 mg per day. The oyster article also covers food-safety risks of raw oysters.

name: Boron + zinc + D3 test-boost stack

angle.text: Supplement and looksmaxxing communities combine these three to raise testosterone for muscle and masculine looks. Each ingredient has some published link to hormone physiology, but the combination has no trial.

summary: Boron, zinc and D3 together as a testosterone stack: each has a plausible hormone link, but the combo has no trial behind it.
note: Zinc beyond sufficiency does not raise testosterone, per Wikipedia.
currentQuick:
A popular supplement stack of boron, zinc and vitamin D3 taken to raise testosterone.
Deficiency of zinc or vitamin D is linked to lower levels; evidence for the stack in people without deficiency was not found.
How it works: Zinc supports testosterone synthesis, vitamin D intake correlates with higher levels, and boron is proposed to influence steroid metabolism.
Risks and caveats: Borates have low mammalian toxicity per Wikipedia, but excess intake of any ingredient is not covered in the sources reviewed.
deepLead:
The boron, zinc and vitamin D3 stack is a combination of over-the-counter supplements taken in the belief that together they raise testosterone. Each ingredient has some published link to hormone physiology, and the combination is discussed in supplement and looksmaxxing communities.
Wikipedia reports that zinc deficiency lowers testosterone while over-supplementation does not change serum testosterone, and that vitamin D intakes around 400 to 1000 IU per day were associated with higher testosterone. Its boron article notes boron is only needed in traces by plants, that borates have low mammalian toxicity, and lists a 1987 study of dietary boron on estrogen and testosterone metabolism in postmenopausal women without giving its findings. Evidence for the three-ingredient stack itself was not found.

name: Soy avoidance

angle.text: Fitness and looksmaxxing communities avoid soy out of concern that phytoestrogens lower testosterone or feminise men. Meta-analyses have found no effect of soy or isoflavones on male hormones.

summary: Avoiding soy to protect testosterone: meta-analyses find no effect of soy or isoflavones on male hormones.
note: Only food-allergy or medical reasons are described as established grounds for avoidance in reviewed sources.
currentQuick:
Some people avoid soy believing its plant estrogens lower testosterone or feminise men.
A 2020 meta-analysis found no effect of soy or isoflavones on male reproductive hormones in healthy people.
How it works: Isoflavones are phytoestrogens that bind estrogen receptors weakly in lab settings; human hormone effects were not found in pooled trials.
Risks and caveats: Avoidance itself has no described harm in the sources; allergies are the established reason to avoid soy.
deepLead:
Soy avoidance is the practice of cutting soy foods from the diet because of fears that their isoflavones, plant compounds classed as phytoestrogens, lower testosterone, raise estrogen or feminise men. The idea circulates widely in fitness and looksmaxxing communities.
Soy products contain the most isoflavones of any common food group. A 2020 meta-analysis by Reed, Camargo and Messina found that neither soy nor isoflavone intake affected male reproductive hormones, and a 2021 review by Messina and colleagues concluded soyfoods do not warrant classification as endocrine disruptors; a separate 2020 review in Nutrients found insufficient clinical evidence of phytoestrogen effects in humans.

name: Plastic / endocrine disruptor avoidance

angle.text: Users swap plastic for glass or steel and avoid certain packaging to protect testosterone and hormone balance. Regulators are tightening limits on these chemicals, but avoidance trials in men are absent.

summary: Dodging BPA and phthalates to protect testosterone: regulators are tightening limits, but avoidance trials in men are absent.
note: Regulatory concern is real; effect of personal avoidance on adult testosterone is untested in reviewed sources.
currentQuick:
Avoiding plastics and endocrine disruptors is meant to protect hormone levels. BPA and phthalates are the chemicals most discussed.
Regulators have restricted BPA, though how much household avoidance changes adult testosterone has not been tested in the sources reviewed.
How it works: BPA acts as a weak estrogen-receptor modulator and can antagonise the androgen receptor at high concentrations; phthalates have antiandrogenic effects in animal data.
Risks and caveats: Substitutes like BPS and BPF have raised their own concerns. Avoidance itself has no described harm.
deepLead:
Plastic and endocrine disruptor avoidance is a lifestyle practice of limiting exposure to BPA, phthalates and similar plastic additives in order to protect testosterone and hormone balance. People swap plastic containers for glass or steel and avoid certain packaged foods and receipts.
Endocrine disruptors are chemicals that can interfere with hormone synthesis, action or elimination. BPA binds estrogen receptors roughly 1,000 to 2,000 times less potently than estradiol, and at high concentrations antagonises the androgen receptor. Wikipedia links endocrine disruptors to reduced sperm quality and fertility and reports phthalates linked to shorter anogenital distance in male infants.

name: Tap water / fluoride avoidance

angle.text: Some appearance-focused users drink and wash with filtered or spring water to avoid fluoride and chlorine, presenting it as part of a skin and health routine. Health bodies back fluoridation, critics dispute it, and no appearance data exist.

summary: Swapping tap for filtered or spring water to dodge fluoride; health bodies back fluoridation, critics dispute it, and no appearance data exist.
note: Contested public-health topic; no evidence for appearance benefit.
currentQuick:
Some people avoid tap water to avoid fluoride, believing it is unhealthy. Health bodies such as the WHO and CDC support fluoridation at recommended levels, while critics dispute its benefit and safety.
No study has tested whether avoiding fluoride changes how someone looks.
How it works: People use filters, bottled or spring water. Fluoride is added to public water to reduce tooth decay.
Risks and caveats: Fluoridation's documented adverse effect at recommended levels is mostly mild dental fluorosis; neurodevelopment concerns are debated and a 2024 US court ruling addressed IQ risk. Reduced fluoride exposure is associated with more cavities in some reviews.
deepLead:
Tap water / fluoride avoidance is a lifestyle practice in which people drink and sometimes wash with filtered, bottled or spring water instead of municipal tap water, mainly to avoid fluoride, and sometimes chlorine. In appearance-focused communities it is presented as part of a health-and-skin routine.
Water fluoridation is the controlled addition of fluoride to public water supplies to reduce tooth decay; the US recommended level is 0.7 mg/L. Health bodies including the WHO, the FDI World Dental Federation and the US CDC endorse it as safe and effective at recommended levels, while opponents argue the benefit is small and that safety is uncertain. No published study was found that tests fluoride avoidance for facial appearance.

name: Filtered / spring water

chain: Filter or spring water in place of tap
angle.text: Some people drink filtered or bottled spring water to avoid fluoride and chlorine, hoping for cleaner skin and general health. Tap water is heavily regulated and no appearance benefit has been documented.

summary: Drinking filtered or spring water to avoid fluoride and chlorine; tap water is heavily regulated and no appearance benefit is documented.
note: Spring water can contain arsenic; filters need maintenance.
currentQuick:
Some people drink filtered or bottled spring water instead of tap water to avoid fluoride and chlorine.
No human study has tested it for skin or facial appearance.
How it works: Home filters (carbon, membrane) or bottled water from natural springs replace municipal supply.
Risks and caveats: Some springs contain arsenic, bottled water has been found to contain microplastics, and poorly maintained filters have been linked to outbreaks. Bottled water costs much more than tap.
deepLead:
Filtered or spring water is drinking water treated with a home filter or bought bottled from a spring, used by some people in place of tap water to avoid fluoride and chlorine.
Spring water is groundwater emerging naturally from an aquifer; its dissolved mineral content varies, and some springs contain arsenic above the WHO 10 ppb standard. Tap water in developed countries is described as heavily tested, and bottled water is regulated as a packaged food in the US. No published study was found testing filtered or spring water for facial appearance.

name: Alcohol avoidance (sober maxxing)

angle.text: Sober maxxers quit alcohol to get clearer, less puffy skin and better sleep. Alcohol's health effects are well documented; improvement in appearance after quitting has not been formally tested.

summary: Quitting alcohol for clearer skin; alcohol carries well-documented health risks, but appearance gains are untested.
note: Heavy drinkers should not stop abruptly without medical advice.
currentQuick:
Some people quit alcohol hoping for better-looking skin and general health.
Health benefits of abstinence such as better sleep and liver recovery are reported, but no study has measured facial appearance specifically.
How it works: Abstaining removes ethanol and its metabolite acetaldehyde, which is linked to flushing and DNA damage.
Risks and caveats: Alcohol is an IARC Group 1 carcinogen. Medical guidance notes that withdrawal in dependent drinkers can be dangerous.
deepLead:
Alcohol avoidance, sometimes called sober maxxing, is the practice of quitting or abstaining from alcohol, in appearance communities often for the stated aim of improving skin.
The IARC classifies ethanol as a Group 1 carcinogen, and the WHO has stated that no level of alcohol consumption is free of health risks. Reported benefits of sustained abstinence include better sleep, reversal of early fatty liver disease and lower blood pressure. No published study was found testing alcohol abstinence for facial appearance.

name: Quitting smoking / vaping

angle.text: Appearance communities cite quitting to slow premature skin aging, since smoker's face brings a distinctive wrinkle pattern and sallow tone. Smoker's face is well documented; how much of it reverses after quitting is thinly studied.

summary: Quitting smoking or vaping to slow skin aging; smoker's face is documented, quitting's facial reversal is thinly studied.
note: Nicotine cessation: seek medical support if needed.
currentQuick:
Smokers show a characteristic aged look: wrinkles and grey, sallow skin. Some people quit hoping to look younger.
Observational data show the features are less common in former smokers, but reversal is not well established.
How it works: Smoking raises collagen-degrading enzymes, narrows blood vessels and increases oxidative stress.
Risks and caveats: Smoking carries major documented harms including cancers, heart and lung disease. Quitting is associated with falling lung cancer risk over years.
deepLead:
Quitting smoking or vaping is a practice appearance communities cite for reducing premature skin aging. Smoker's face describes facial changes seen in smokers, including a characteristic wrinkle pattern and sallow grey skin tone.
A 1985 BMJ study by D. Model reported certain facial features in about 46% of continuing smokers and 8% of former smokers who had smoked for a decade. Proposed mechanisms include raised matrix metalloproteinases degrading collagen and elastin, vasoconstriction and oxidative stress. The sources reviewed do not address vaping and skin.

name: Caffeine avoidance

angle.text: Users cut caffeine hoping for less facial puffiness and better sleep, which they link to a fresher look. Caffeine's effects on sleep are documented; the effect on puffiness is untested.

summary: Dropping caffeine to reduce puffiness and improve sleep; sleep effects are documented, puffiness is untested.
note: Withdrawal headaches are common for a day or so.
currentQuick:
Some people avoid caffeine hoping for a less puffy face and better sleep.
Caffeine can disrupt sleep, but no study links avoiding it to reduced facial puffiness.
How it works: Caffeine blocks adenosine receptors, promoting wakefulness and a brief diuretic effect in non-habitual users.
Risks and caveats: Quitting can cause withdrawal symptoms such as headache and fatigue for a short time.
deepLead:
Caffeine avoidance is cutting out coffee, tea and energy drinks, in appearance communities often for the stated aim of reducing facial puffiness and improving sleep.
Caffeine is a central nervous system stimulant that can delay or prevent sleep, and large acute doses of about 250 to 300 mg temporarily increase urine output mainly in people who have abstained, while regular users develop tolerance. No published study was found testing caffeine avoidance for facial puffiness.

name: Coffee for skin / Cold brew

angle.text: Appearance communities promote coffee and cold brew, drunk or applied topically, for skin and looks. General health data on coffee exist; the skin claims are untested.

summary: Coffee and cold brew pitched for skin; general health data exist but skin claims are untested here.
note: Little skin-specific evidence found.
currentQuick:
Coffee and cold brew are discussed online as skin helpers.
General health research on coffee exists, but nothing reviewed addresses skin appearance.
How it works: Cold brew is steeped in cold water, yielding lower acidity; no skin mechanism is documented in the sources reviewed.
Risks and caveats: Caffeine can cause anxiety or sleep disruption at high intakes, and pregnancy limits apply.
deepLead:
Coffee for skin / cold brew refers to claims in appearance communities about coffee, including cold brew, and skin or looks, whether by drinking or topical use.
Cold brew is made by steeping coarse grounds in cold or room-temperature water for about 4 to 24 hours; research reports lower titratable acidity than hot coffee. A 2017 umbrella review found coffee generally safe at usual intakes. The sources reviewed do not discuss skin, topical use, cellulite or under-eye effects of coffee.

name: Nutritional yeast / B-vitamin loading

chain: Supports skin, hair and nail cells
angle.text: Users eat fortified nutritional yeast or stack B-complex in the hope of better skin, hair and nails. The vitamins' roles are established, but their cosmetic payoff beyond correcting a deficiency is unstudied.

summary: Eating fortified yeast flakes or stacking B-complex for skin and hair; the vitamins are real, the cosmetic payoff is unstudied.
note: High-dose biotin can distort some lab test results.
currentQuick:
Nutritional yeast is a deactivated yeast eaten as a cheesy seasoning, and fortified versions contain large amounts of B vitamins. Some people in appearance communities use it or B-complex supplements hoping for better skin, hair and nails.
No clinical trial has tested the practice for cosmetic results. Evidence on individual vitamins such as biotin is limited in people who are not deficient.
How it works: B vitamins take part in normal skin and hair metabolism, and deficiency of some, such as biotin, can cause hair thinning, brittle nails or rash. Proponents extend this to the idea that extra intake improves appearance in people who are not deficient; that extension has not been tested in trials.
Risks and caveats: Nutritional yeast is a food and generally regarded as low risk. High-dose biotin supplements can interfere with some blood tests, including thyroid tests, per an FDA safety communication, and high niacin intake can cause flushing.
deepLead:
Nutritional yeast, informally called "nooch", is a deactivated yeast, usually a strain of Saccharomyces cerevisiae, sold as yellow flakes or powder and used in vegan cooking as a cheese-like seasoning . In looksmaxxing and wider wellness circles, "B-vitamin loading" refers to eating nutritional yeast or taking B-complex supplements in generous amounts in the hope of improving skin, hair and nails.
Fortified nutritional yeast can supply several B vitamins in amounts far above the Daily Value per serving, according to manufacturer figures reported on Wikipedia, including thiamine, riboflavin, niacin, vitamin B6 and vitamin B12 . Yeast cannot make B12 itself, so the B12 in such products is added during fortification .
No published clinical trial has tested nutritional yeast or broad B-vitamin loading for cosmetic appearance outcomes. Related evidence concerns single nutrients: for biotin, human evidence for hair and nail benefit in people without deficiency is limited, and high-dose biotin can interfere with some laboratory tests .

name: Heavy cream / butter diet

angle.text: Appearance communities use this high-fat dairy variant of low-carb eating to lose fat and keep meals simple. It has not been trialled for looks.

summary: A very high-fat dairy take on low-carb eating; nobody has trialled it for looks, and butter raises LDL.
note: Very high saturated fat intake raises LDL cholesterol.
currentQuick:
This is a low-carbohydrate approach in which butter and heavy cream provide most calories. It is discussed as a simple high-fat option related to keto.
No studies have tested it specifically for fat loss or appearance outcomes.
How it works: Butter and cream supply fat with almost no carbohydrate, which proponents say helps with fullness and with staying in ketosis. These claims have not been tested for this exact pattern.
Risks and caveats: Butter is high in saturated fat and raises LDL cholesterol relative to plant oils, according to cited reviews. Health bodies such as the NHS advise limiting it. Ketogenic diets can cause constipation, lipid changes and kidney stones.
deepLead:
The heavy cream / butter diet is a high-fat dairy variant of low-carbohydrate eating, in which large amounts of butter and cream supply a major share of calories. It is discussed in appearance communities mainly as a way to lose fat or to keep meals simple while eating very low carbohydrate.
Butter is about 81 percent butterfat and is high in saturated fat, at roughly 51 g per 100 g . Wikipedia reports that replacing plant oils with butter raises LDL cholesterol, which is associated with higher cardiovascular risk, although direct evidence on butter specifically is limited .
No clinical studies of a diet centred on heavy cream and butter for appearance outcomes were located.
